To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of cervical human papillomaviruses infection in women attending the routine cervical cancer screening in a Spanish regional population is high.
the prevalence of HPV infection is high and that the majority of cases are due to multiple HPV types.

(1) the prevalence of HPV infection among women attending routine screening was 81.6%; (2) the most prevalent HPV genotypes were HPV51 (7,8%), HPV16 (8,7%) and HPV52 (5,2%), and (3) the most frequent HPV infection pattern was multiple infection (55,0%).
In summary, our research is concerned with

the importance of the study of HPV genotypes and the multiple infection in women attending a routine screening in a Spanish population, in order to design more effective preventive strategies and thus contribute the fight against cervical neoplasia.
the importance of HPV genotyping in routine cervical cancer screening in order to identify the HPV genotypes that are most prevalent in our community.
the need to continue with the screening programs and the need to improve the vaccination programs in Spain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
HPV is an important factor in cervical cancer, but it is not the sole cause of the disease.
HPV infection is highly prevalent in women who attend routine screening in our region.
the prevalence of HPV infection is high in women attending routine screening, and the most common HPV types were HPV16 and HPV51.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
HPV infection is very common in our population, with multiple infections being very frequent.
the prevalence and distribution patterns of HPV genotypes are different from those reported in other populations.
HPV infection in cervical cancer screening is very high and that the prevalence of high-risk HPV types is high in all cytological groups, even in the group with normal cytology.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the HPV vaccine has the potential to prevent the vast majority of cervical cancers, but it must be given before exposure to HPV.
the prevalence of HPV infection and the distribution of HPV genotypes in our region are similar to those reported in other Spanish and European countries.
HPV testing should be included in routine cervical cancer screening.
